paper.title: Compositional Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models via Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery
paper.abstract:
Abstract Removing copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified concepts from a
deployed text-to-image diffusion model is now a practical
requirement.
Weight-editing methods can suppress fixed targets, but they require
per-target retraining and modify the model checkpoint. Training-free
methods, on the other hand, are deployment-friendly, but they
suffer from text-side routing failures on compositional prompts.
In such prompts, the erase target may be invoked through a related
class rather than its lexical name, and its modifiers may migrate
onto preserved objects.
This paper proposes Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery
(HGSS), a training-free framework for compositional concept
erasure. The framework lifts both the routing signal and the edit
operator used by text-side erasure. First, hierarchical span
grounding resolves erase-target spans through lexical, taxonomic,
and semantic evidence, while guarding against broad-hypernym and
compound-head false positives. Second, dynamic attribute binding
refines the text conditioning during early denoising via a
counterfactual reference and a preserve-aware cross-attention
objective, keeping surviving attribute–noun bindings intact.
HGSS selectively removes the erase target without updating
model weights or adding learned parameters.
On SEE, HGSS cuts hierarchical evasion from 29.54 29.54 to 10.02 10.02 and roughly halves pairwise attribute leakage, achieving the best
Neighbor E E and Attr P P scores among the reported erasure
methods. On
UnlearnCanvas, HGSS slightly improves the six-metric average
over the matched SS baseline, reaching state-of-the-art.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Removing copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified concepts from a deployed text-to-image diffusion model [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] is now a practical requirement. Real prompts, however, are compositional. A target may be invoked through hierarchical or implicit reference, and modifiers often remain bound to objects that the erasure procedure is trying to remove. The requirement is especially sharp for training-free erasure, where the deployed U-Net is left untouched and the intervention happens only through the text-conditioning stream. Existing methods occupy two deployment regimes. Weight-editing methods—ESD [ Gandikota et al.(2023)Gandikota, Materzyńska, Fiotto-Kaufman, and Bau ] , UCE [ Gandikota et al.(2024)Gandikota, Orgad, Belinkov, Materzyńska, and Bau ] , MACE [ Lu et al.(2024)Lu, Wang, Li, Liu, and Kong ] , and related approaches (Sec. 2 )—can be strong on fixed targets. However, they modify the model or attach learned modules, and each edit incurs a training, storage, and distribution-shift cost. Training-free methods—SLD [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] , SAFREE [ Yoon et al.(2025)Yoon, Yu, Patil, Yao, and Bansal ] , and Semantic Surgery (SS) [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] —are lighter: the same checkpoint can serve many erase targets on demand. Their bottleneck is that the edit must be computed from the prompt itself. Any routing error in the text side therefore becomes an erasure failure. SS [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] , a strong training-free representative, detects erase-related prompt terms via a similarity-based concept-presence kernel and subtracts a weighted direction from the conditioning hidden states. This handles the literal safety–quality slice of I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] . Two failure modes, however, become apparent on the compositional prompts of the recent SEE benchmark [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] , and neither is reliably addressed by tuning edit strength: 1. Hierarchical evasion. When the prompt does not lexicalize the erase target, similarity-based selection misses descendants of the target. For example, the prompt “a poodle running in the park” under target “mammal” still produces a mammal, because “poodle” is not lexically matched. The parent-to-child case is ambiguous in the opposite direction: “flower” may instantiate the fine-grained target “rose”, and routing the edit through the parent risks suppressing non-target flowers. On the SEE evasion axis, SS remained vulnerable, with a 29.54 29.54 average despite strong neighboring erasure. 2. Attribute leakage. Cross-attention text-side subtraction projects an aggregate direction and cannot determine whether a modifier such as “blue” belongs to the target noun or to a preserved one. As a result, attributes of the target can migrate onto preserved objects: “a blue car next to a dog” becomes a blue dog . On the SEE attribute-leakage axis, SS’s pairwise CLIP Attr E E exceeded twice that of weight-edit baselines (Attr P P was roughly 1.4 × 1.4\times theirs). These two failures, visualised in Figure 1 , share a structural cause. SS treats the prompt as a set of candidate terms and routes a single concept direction through lexical–CLIP similarity. This primitive represents neither the hierarchy that relates a target to its descendants nor the binding that ties an attribute to its noun. A larger SS subtraction can sharpen the edit on lexicalized targets. It cannot, however, recover an unselected descendant token or decide which noun a modifier should remain bound to. The remedy must therefore replace the structural primitives rather than re-tune the existing scalars.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: This paper proposes Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery (HGSS), a training-free framework for compositional concept erasure. Its contributions are: 1. A structural framing for compositional erasure. Existing training-free erasure methods treat prompt terms as loosely related routing cues. HGSS instead views concept erasure as the inverse objective to compositional generation. The framework keeps the SS coarse edit interface, but replaces its lexical routing and static conditioning primitives. The two replacements remain training-free: neither introduces learned parameters nor per-concept hand-coded rules. 2. Hierarchical span grounding. To decide what to edit, HGSS introduces a resolver for erase-target spans (Sec. 3.3 ). The resolver combines lexical matches, WordNet-backed taxonomic evidence, and semantic fallback. Broad-hypernym and compound-head guards reduce false positives on preserved objects. 3. Dynamic attribute binding. To decide how the edit evolves, HGSS introduces a per-step conditioning update for early denoising (Sec. 3.4 ). A counterfactual reference defines the target-removed state. An asymmetric attention objective protects preserve spans and suppresses leakage from erase-target spans. 4. Evaluation across complementary axes. The experiments evaluate the two structural mechanisms on compositional side effects, style/object unlearning, and direct lexical safety compatibility. Across the three axes, the resolver and dynamic binding reduce compositional side effects while broadly preserving image quality and the safety capability of the inherited coarse edit. Ablations separate the resolver from dynamic binding (Sec. 4 ). Taken together, the two structural mechanisms view erasure as an inverse objective to compositional generation . Rather than binding every prompt entity correctly, the framework first routes the erase target and its descendants into the edit set, then stabilises the surviving preserve-side bindings during denoising. The grounding cascade and the dynamic-binding update are implemented as a plug-in module for training-free, text-side concept erasure.

sections.heading: Parameter-modifying concept erasure.
sections.text: A large body of work edits the diffusion model itself to remove a target concept. Fine-tuning objectives steer the generator away from the target distribution. ESD [ Gandikota et al.(2023)Gandikota, Materzyńska, Fiotto-Kaufman, and Bau ] fine-tunes U-Net attention with a negative-guidance loss, Concept Ablation [ Kumari et al.(2023)Kumari, Zhang, Wang, Shechtman, Zhang, and Zhu ] matches a surrogate concept, and AdvUnlearn [ Zhang et al.(2024c)Zhang, Chen, Jia, Zhang, Fan, Liu, Hong, Ding, and Liu ] optimises adversarial robustness during erasure. Closed-form and low-rank weight edits act directly on cross-attention projections without full fine-tuning. UCE [ Gandikota et al.(2024)Gandikota, Orgad, Belinkov, Materzyńska, and Bau ] and RECE [ Gong et al.(2024)Gong, Chen, Wei, Chen, and Jiang ] apply closed-form edits, MACE [ Lu et al.(2024)Lu, Wang, Li, Liu, and Kong ] targets many concepts jointly, and SPM [ Lyu et al.(2024)Lyu, Yang, Hong, Chen, Jin, He, Xue, Han, and Ding ] uses one-dimensional adapters. Sparsity- and saliency-guided edits localise the intervention to a subset of parameters. SalUn [ Fan et al.(2024)Fan, Liu, Zhang, Wong, Wei, and Liu ] uses gradient-based weight saliency, SAeUron [ Cywiński and Deja(2025) ] edits sparse-autoencoder features, and ConceptPrune [ Chavhan et al.(2025)Chavhan, Li, and Hospedales ] prunes skilled neurons. Locality-oriented and representation-space methods reduce collateral damage by constraining where the edit applies. CPE [ Lee et al.(2025b)Lee, Lim, Lee, Kang, and Chun ] introduces residual attention gates, GLoCE [ Lee et al.(2025a)Lee, Lim, and Chun ] gates a training-free low-rank adaptation, and AdaVD [ Wang et al.(2025)Wang, Li, Mu, Hao, Liu, Wang, and He ] edits the value space along orthogonal complements. A further line refines target geometry : AGE [ Bui et al.(2025)Bui, Vu, Vuong, Le, Montague, Abraham, Kim, and Phung ] identifies which concepts to push erased samples toward, while CoGFD [ Nie et al.(2025)Nie, Yao, Liu, Wang, and Bian ] explicitly handles combinations of erase targets rather than single nouns. These methods exploit additional parameter capacity to retain preserve-side fidelity, but require per-target training and modified checkpoints.

sections.heading: Training-free and inference-time erasure.
sections.text: Training-free erasure preserves the base generator and intervenes only at sampling time. SLD [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] modifies classifier-free guidance using a safety prompt; SAFREE [ Yoon et al.(2025)Yoon, Yu, Patil, Yao, and Bansal ] projects text embeddings away from unsafe directions before they enter the U-Net. TraSCE [ Jain et al.(2024)Jain, Kobayashi, Shibuya, Takida, Memon, Togelius, and Mitsufuji ] steers the denoising trajectory away from harmful regions via a localised loss-based guidance. Semantic Surgery (SS) [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] subtracts a similarity-weighted concept direction from the conditioning hidden states. These methods are deployment-friendly since the same checkpoint serves many erase targets on demand, but their edits are only as reliable as the text-side signals that select the edited span. When the target is reached through a related class, a semantic variant, or an entangled attribute phrase, a single conditioning-time subtraction can fail in two ways. It can miss the routing path entirely, or remove content beyond the intended span.

sections.heading: Side effects and robustness.
sections.text: Early erasure evaluations emphasise literal unsafe-content removal and clean-set image quality, exemplified by I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] with NudeNet-based scoring. UnlearnCanvas [ Zhang et al.(2024b)Zhang, Fan, Zhang, Yao, Jia, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Kompella, Liu, and Liu ] expands this view to style and object unlearning across 60 60 styles and 20 20 object classes. SEE [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] factors side effects into neighboring impact , hierarchical evasion , and attribute leakage , each with its own protocol. A complementary line stress-tests erased models with adversarial prompts: Ring-A-Bell [ Tsai et al.(2024)Tsai, Hsu, Xie, Lin, Chen, Li, Chen, Yu, and Huang ] , UnlearnDiffAtk [ Zhang et al.(2024d)Zhang, Jia, Chen, Chen, Zhang, Liu, Ding, and Liu ] , MMA-Diffusion [ Yang et al.(2024)Yang, Gao, Wang, Ho, Xu, and Xu ] , and P4D [ Chin et al.(2024)Chin, Jiang, Huang, Chen, and Chiu ] .

sections.heading: Text-side compositional control.
sections.text: A separate line edits text conditioning states during sampling to repair compositional generation failures. Prompt-to-Prompt [ Hertz et al.(2023)Hertz, Mokady, Tenenbaum, Aberman, Pritch, and Cohen-Or ] swaps cross-attention maps between related prompts. Attend-and-Excite [ Chefer et al.(2023)Chefer, Alaluf, Vinker, Wolf, and Cohen-Or ] strengthens the attention of subject tokens that risk being neglected. Structure Diffusion [ Feng et al.(2023)Feng, He, Fu, Jampani, Akula, Narayana, Basu, Wang, and Wang ] incorporates linguistic structure into the guidance computation, and DATE [ Na et al.(2025)Na, Park, Sim, Shin, Bae, Kang, Kwon, Kang, and Moon ] updates the text embedding per denoising step to correct attribute–object misbinding. SynGen [ Rassin et al.(2023)Rassin, Hirsch, Glickman, Ravfogel, Goldberg, and Chechik ] introduces a positive–negative cross-attention loss that aligns each attribute’s attention with the noun it modifies. HGSS sits at the intersection of these lines by keeping the deployment advantage of training-free erasure but replacing the similarity-only routing used by prior inference-time methods with a hierarchical span grounding cascade. From text-side compositional control, HGSS reuses attribute–object binding primitives on the preserve side. HGSS inverts that framework’s objective by first routing target spans and descendants into the edit set, then re-applying binding control only to surviving spans, thereby treating concept erasure as the inverse objective to compositional generation , motivating the counterfactual reference and preserve-restricted attention pair in Sec. 3.4 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries and Notation
sections.text: HGSS is described here in the setting of a latent text-to-image diffusion model with a frozen autoencoder, a CLIP text encoder [ Radford et al.(2021)Radford, Kim, Hallacy, Ramesh, Goh, Agarwal, Sastry, Askell, Mishkin, Clark, Krueger, and Sutskever ] ℰ \mathcal{E} , and a U-Net ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} trained for ϵ \epsilon -prediction [ Ho et al.(2020)Ho, Jain, and Abbeel ] . Given a prompt p p , the text encoder returns conditioning hidden states c = ℰ ⁡ ( p ) ∈ ℝ L × d c=\mathcal{E}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} . At inference, a DDIM [ Song et al.(2021)Song, Meng, and Ermon ] schedule iteratively denoises a latent z T z_{T} over T = 50 T{=}50 steps using classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ Ho and Salimans(2022) ] with scale w w . In our experiments, this instantiation is Stable Diffusion v1.4 [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] . A concept-erasure method takes c c , an erase target T e T_{e} , and an optional preserve target T p T_{p} . It returns an edited conditioning c ~ \tilde{c} such that the sampled image no longer depicts T e T_{e} while the non-target content remains intact. In the SS base, selection is similarity-driven and spans contribute uniformly. When preserve spans are grounded, the aggregated erase direction is projected onto the orthogonal complement of the weighted preserve direction before subtraction, at a fixed unit scale. HGSS determines which spans enter S S and their weights and how the edited conditioning evolves during sampling , and does not introduce any new scalar at the coarse-edit interface.

sections.heading: 3.2 Overview of HGSS
sections.text: HGSS makes two structural changes to the coarse-edit pipeline, which form two halves of the framework. Structured routing decides what to edit by using hierarchical span grounding instead of token-level similarity (Sec. 3.3 ). Structured edit decides how the edit evolves via dynamic attribute binding during denoising, rather than a single conditioning subtraction (Sec. 3.4 ). The two modules address hierarchical evasion and attribute leakage asymmetrically: structured routing supplies the main erase-side correction, while structured edit stabilises preserve-side bindings so the routing gain is not paid for by leakage onto surviving nouns. The two halves and the SS-inherited coarse edit between them comprise the visual pipeline in Figure 2 . Given ( p , T e , T p ) (p,T_{e},T_{p}) , HGSS executes three inference stages (Figure 2 ; full algorithm in App. A.3): 1. Ground. The span-grounding module returns weighted erase spans 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} and preserve spans 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} in the prompt, using lexical, hierarchical, and semantic evidence. 2. Coarse edit. The coarse edit (Eq. ( 1 )) is applied using the grounded erase spans when available and falls back to the base similarity-driven selection otherwise, producing the static anchor c ~ \tilde{c} . 3. Bind. A text-side localization module builds counterfactual references and preserve-side attribute anchors; during denoising, the dynamic update refines the live conditioning c ¯ \bar{c} with attention and CLIP losses. Figure 2: HGSS pipeline. HGSS surrounds the SS-inherited weighted coarse edit (Eq. ( 1 )) with two training-free modules. Hierarchical Span Grounding produces the weighted edit plan from lexical, taxonomic, and semantic evidence, gated by broad-hypernym and compound-head guards (Sec. 3.3 ). Dynamic Attribute Binding stabilises the preserve-side bindings exposed by the resolver-expanded erase set, refining the live conditioning during the first 0.6 0.6 fraction of DDIM iterations via an asymmetric preserve-aware cross-attention objective (Sec. 3.4 ). The U-Net and the CLIP text encoder remain frozen throughout.

sections.heading: 3.3 Hierarchical Span Grounding
sections.text: This module addresses hierarchical evasion : given prompt p p and target T e T_{e} , it returns the prompt spans that should be treated as erase-positive evidence, including spans that are hierarchical descendants of T e T_{e} when T e T_{e} itself does not appear lexically in p p . SS solves this with CLIP similarity alone, which is unreliable when T e T_{e} is not lexicalized. HGSS replaces this similarity-only test with a deterministic cascade that emits weighted (span, relation, confidence) tuples and removes false positives via guard rules so that the remaining tuples become the weighted erase set 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} and, by complement, the preserve set 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} .

sections.heading: Cascade.
sections.text: The cascade consults three categories of evidence in order of signal reliability: lexical, taxonomic, and semantic. Lexical evidence provides high precision. Taxonomic evidence expands recall when lexical matches fail. And, semantic fallback handles open-vocabulary concepts beyond the lexicon. These three categories are visualised as the three labelled icons in Box 2 of Figure 2 and are realised through four sources, consulted in priority order. The first source that emits a confident candidate determines the relation label. (1) Lexical evidence tests exact equality, substring containment, and tokenized head-noun match between prompt term t k t_{k} and T e T_{e} . Exact matches are labelled self . (2a) Taxonomic backoff uses WordNet [ Miller(1995) ] to supply non-lexical evidence when lexical matching fails. The resolver looks up synsets for t k t_{k} and T e T_{e} and runs a breadth-first traversal of the hypernym/hyponym directed acyclic graph (DAG) with max depth 12 12 . The closest valid relation is classified as descendant / child (force-include), parent / parent-like , or sibling via shared hypernyms. A broad-hypernym guard suppresses generic ancestors ( entity , object , whole , artifact , organism , …) so that “car” and “apple” do not become hierarchically related through the root of the WordNet DAG. (2b) Activity bridge (a taxonomic refinement) handles verb-style targets and gerund-derived identifiers by expanding each candidate through WordNet derivational links into verb, gerund, and nominal variants, then applying the same relation and CLIP checks. The expansion is generated per prompt rather than taken from a hand-curated activity lexicon. (3) Semantic fallback admits a candidate when its CLIP cosine similarity to T e T_{e} exceeds a stage-specific threshold (distinct values for primary erase, derived modifiers, and activity targets; full settings are in App. B.1). This stage handles out-of-WordNet concepts (style names, brand names) without hand-curated lists.

sections.heading: Guards.
sections.text: Two guard rules reduce the most common false-positive patterns in our development set: • Compound-head guard. For a compound noun t k = w 1 ​ w 2 ​ … ​ w n t_{k}=w_{1}\,w_{2}\,\ldots\,w_{n} , the derived head w n w_{n} is only erased if the full compound t k t_{k} has an erase-positive relation to T e T_{e} . A relation between only w n w_{n} and T e T_{e} in isolation will not necessarily trigger erasure. This prevents “ baseball bat ” from triggering erasure under a generic “mammal” target: the derived head “bat” is a mammal in WordNet, but the full compound “baseball bat” does not bear a descendant relation to mammal . • Self-suppression. If the prompt lexicalizes a descendant of T e T_{e} (the resolver returns a descendant / child candidate), the self candidate corresponding to T e T_{e} itself is suppressed to avoid double-counting when T e T_{e} is also a prompt token.

sections.heading: The edit plan.
sections.text: The resolver returns a weighted erase set 𝒜 E = { ( t k , ω k ) } k \mathcal{A}_{E}=\{(t_{k},\omega_{k})\}_{k} and an analogously weighted preserve set 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} . The weight ω k \omega_{k} reflects the cascade’s confidence in candidate t k t_{k} : force-included relations ( self , descendant , child ) contribute at a default full weight; threshold-admitted candidates contribute at their cascade-stage confidence score. All other candidates must clear a similarity-confidence threshold and a separate preserve-strength floor that protects against weakly related nouns. When the user provides an explicit preserve target T p T_{p} (as in SEE and UnlearnCanvas protocols), the resolver anchors T p T_{p} ’s span in 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} ; otherwise 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} is the complement of 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} within the prompt. All threshold values were fixed once during development and not tuned on SEE or UnlearnCanvas; exact values are listed in App. B.1. The role separation between span grounding and dynamic binding is evaluated through module-level diagnostic ablations in Sec. 4.5 .

sections.heading: Worked example.
sections.text: Under target “mammal”, the resolver marks “poodle” (in “a poodle running in the park”) as a force-included descendant span via WordNet backoff. The compound-head guard, however, suppresses “bat” in “a baseball bat on the kitchen counter” because the full compound does not bear an erase-positive relation. The full cascade trace is in App. A.1.

sections.heading: 3.4 Dynamic Attribute Binding
sections.text: Dynamic Attribute Binding is not intended to be a standalone erasure mechanism. It refines the live conditioning during early DDIM steps so that, after the resolver-grounded coarse edit, the modifier–noun bindings on spans that should survive the erasure remain intact. A small gradient correction is applied to the conditioning embeddings during early DDIM steps, when object layout and attribute binding are still being established. The update combines two parts: a per-token counterfactual reference and a per-step composite loss. The reference anchors what each token position should encode after T e T_{e} is removed. The composite loss pulls each preserved (modifier, head-noun) pair together while pushing preserve-side keys away from the residue left by the coarse edit.

sections.heading: Design rationale.
sections.text: The four loss components in Eq. ( 3 ) (introduced below) are not interchangeable. Each constrains a distinct level of the conditioning pipeline. The update concentrates in early denoising, where object layout and cross-attention bindings are most malleable. Detailed motivation for each component (the symmetric-KL choices for the attention losses, the residual CLIP-space target penalty, and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} prior anchor) is in App. A.2.

sections.heading: (b) Leakage-suppression loss ℒ neg ( t ) \mathcal{L}_{\text{neg}}^{(t)} .
sections.text: Building on the positive/negative attention principle of SynGen [ Rassin et al.(2023)Rassin, Hirsch, Glickman, Ravfogel, Goldberg, and Chechik ] , the second term pushes each preserve attribute key away from the rest of the prompt. sections.text: HGSS and the training-free baselines are evaluated as drop-in text-side modifiers of Stable Diffusion v1.4 [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] with the DDIM sampler at 50 50 inference steps, classifier-free guidance scale 7.5 7.5 , image resolution 512 × 512 512{\times}512 . No fine-tuning or distillation is performed. For controlled comparison, all SS baselines are evaluated with visual feedback disabled (no-VF). HGSS does not use visual feedback, so the SS → \rightarrow HGSS comparison isolates the two proposed modules under the same coarse text-side edit interface. All reported SS and HGSS rows use the same evaluation protocol and the same benchmark-specific coarse-edit operating point. For compositional erasure (SEE, UnlearnCanvas) the SS coarse-edit operating point is β = − 0.12 \beta{=}{-}0.12 ; for direct safety erasure (I2P) it is β = − 0.06 \beta{=}{-}0.06 , matching the original SS safety operating point. In every setting HGSS introduces no new hyperparameter at this interface and runs at exactly the same β \beta as the matched SS baseline . Per-step refinements use the window [ 0 , 0.6 ​ T ] [0,\,0.6T] and interval Δ ​ t = 10 \Delta t{=}10 . The step size is η = 0.5 \eta{=}0.5 . The loss weights are ( λ bind , λ neg , λ tgt , λ prior ) = ( 0.4 , 0.1 , 1.0 , 0.02 ) (\lambda_{\text{bind}},\lambda_{\text{neg}},\lambda_{\text{tgt}},\lambda_{\text{prior}}){=}(0.4,\,0.1,\,1.0,\,0.02) of Sec. 3.4.2 ; identical settings are used on every benchmark, and the update target is the live conditioning embedding c ¯ \bar{c} . sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: Three complementary benchmarks were used. (i) SEE [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] served as the primary diagnostic benchmark. Its three side-effect axes isolate the compositional failures targeted by HGSS: neighboring impact (SEE Table 2), evasion (SEE Table 3), and attribute leakage (SEE Table 4). The benchmark spans 11 11 super-categories with 79 79 base objects and 5,056 5{,}056 compositional variants. The official CLIP-based scoring protocol was followed and metrics were reported in the paper direction ( ↓ \downarrow for erase/evasion/leakage; ↑ \uparrow for preserve). Neighbor E E measures residual target evidence on erase-side prompts, while Neighbor P P measures preservation of related non-target concepts. Evasion measures target reappearance through hierarchical or related-class prompts. Attr E E and Attr P P measure pairwise attribute leakage on erase and preserve sides. (ii) UnlearnCanvas [ Zhang et al.(2024b)Zhang, Fan, Zhang, Yao, Jia, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Kompella, Liu, and Liu ] measures style and object unlearning quality. The evaluation covers the 50 50 style targets and 20 20 object targets defined by the official benchmark protocol (selected from the 60 60 -style UnlearnCanvas dataset). The reported metrics are the standard unlearning accuracy (UA), in-domain retention accuracy (IRA), and cross-domain retention accuracy (CRA) triple, with the six-metric average across style and object axes. FID was computed using a regenerated reference set with five images per combination. The SS and HGSS rows are therefore strictly comparable. UA measures target removal. IRA and CRA measure retention on in-domain and cross-domain non-target generations. (iii) I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] measures direct safety erasure. Per-class NudeNet detection counts are taken under the standard paper8 + threshold=0.6 protocol on all 4,703 4{,}703 I2P prompts across eight body-part classes. MS-COCO-30K FID and CLIP are reported as image-quality sanity checks.

sections.text: Table 5 shows a clean division of labour. Grounding improves erasure , cutting Neighbor E E , Evasion, and Attr P P substantially over Base Coarse Surgery at the cost of preserve-side Neighbor P P . Binding alone is not erasure . sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper introduced HGSS, a training-free correction to text-side concept erasure for text-to-image diffusion models. Compositional erasure needs both target routing and preserve-side binding control. Hierarchical span grounding (what to edit) and dynamic attribute binding (how the edit evolves) together cast erasure as the inverse objective to compositional generation. Experiments on SEE and UnlearnCanvas support this view.

Weight-editing methods can suppress fixed targets, but they require per-target retraining and modify the model checkpoint. Training-free methods, on the other hand, are deployment-friendly, but they suffer from text-side routing failures on compositional prompts. In such prompts, the erase target may be invoked through a related class rather than its lexical name, and its modifiers may migrate onto preserved objects. This paper proposes Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery (HGSS), a training-free framework for compositional concept erasure. The framework lifts both the routing signal and the edit operator used by text-side erasure. First, hierarchical span grounding resolves erase-target spans through lexical, taxonomic, and semantic evidence, while guarding against broad-hypernym and compound-head false positives. Second, dynamic attribute binding refines the text conditioning during early denoising via a counterfactual reference and a preserve-aware cross-attention objective, keeping surviving attribute–noun bindings intact. HGSS selectively removes the erase target without updating model weights or adding learned parameters. On SEE, HGSS cuts hierarchical evasion from 29.54 29.54 to 10.02 10.02 and roughly halves pairwise attribute leakage, achieving the best Neighbor E E and Attr P P scores among the reported erasure methods. On UnlearnCanvas, HGSS slightly improves the six-metric average over the matched SS baseline, reaching state-of-the-art. † † affiliation: Department of Computer Science Virginia Tech Alexandria, Virginia, USA † † affiliation: Verisign, Inc. Bottom: under erase target “car”, ESD can retain the target, while SS removes it but transfers the target attribute to the preserved tree. HGSS removes the target concept while preserving non-target content. 1 Introduction Removing copyrighted, unsafe, or user-specified concepts from a deployed text-to-image diffusion model [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] is now a practical requirement. Real prompts, however, are compositional. A target may be invoked through hierarchical or implicit reference, and modifiers often remain bound to objects that the erasure procedure is trying to remove. The requirement is especially sharp for training-free erasure, where the deployed U-Net is left untouched and the intervention happens only through the text-conditioning stream. Existing methods occupy two deployment regimes. Weight-editing methods—ESD [ Gandikota et al.(2023)Gandikota, Materzyńska, Fiotto-Kaufman, and Bau ] , UCE [ Gandikota et al.(2024)Gandikota, Orgad, Belinkov, Materzyńska, and Bau ] , MACE [ Lu et al.(2024)Lu, Wang, Li, Liu, and Kong ] , and related approaches (Sec. 2 )—can be strong on fixed targets. However, they modify the model or attach learned modules, and each edit incurs a training, storage, and distribution-shift cost. Training-free methods—SLD [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] , SAFREE [ Yoon et al.(2025)Yoon, Yu, Patil, Yao, and Bansal ] , and Semantic Surgery (SS) [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] —are lighter: the same checkpoint can serve many erase targets on demand. Their bottleneck is that the edit must be computed from the prompt itself. Any routing error in the text side therefore becomes an erasure failure. SS [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] , a strong training-free representative, detects erase-related prompt terms via a similarity-based concept-presence kernel and subtracts a weighted direction from the conditioning hidden states. This handles the literal safety–quality slice of I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] . Two failure modes, however, become apparent on the compositional prompts of the recent SEE benchmark [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] , and neither is reliably addressed by tuning edit strength: 1. Hierarchical evasion. When the prompt does not lexicalize the erase target, similarity-based selection misses descendants of the target. For example, the prompt “a poodle running in the park” under target “mammal” still produces a mammal, because “poodle” is not lexically matched. The parent-to-child case is ambiguous in the opposite direction: “flower” may instantiate the fine-grained target “rose”, and routing the edit through the parent risks suppressing non-target flowers. On the SEE evasion axis, SS remained vulnerable, with a 29.54 29.54 average despite strong neighboring erasure. 2. Attribute leakage. Cross-attention text-side subtraction projects an aggregate direction and cannot determine whether a modifier such as “blue” belongs to the target noun or to a preserved one. As a result, attributes of the target can migrate onto preserved objects: “a blue car next to a dog” becomes a blue dog . On the SEE attribute-leakage axis, SS’s pairwise CLIP Attr E E exceeded twice that of weight-edit baselines (Attr P P was roughly 1.4 × 1.4\times theirs). These two failures, visualised in Figure 1 , share a structural cause. SS treats the prompt as a set of candidate terms and routes a single concept direction through lexical–CLIP similarity. This primitive represents neither the hierarchy that relates a target to its descendants nor the binding that ties an attribute to its noun. A larger SS subtraction can sharpen the edit on lexicalized targets. It cannot, however, recover an unselected descendant token or decide which noun a modifier should remain bound to. The remedy must therefore replace the structural primitives rather than re-tune the existing scalars. Contributions. This paper proposes Hierarchically Grounded Semantic Surgery (HGSS), a training-free framework for compositional concept erasure. Its contributions are: 1. A structural framing for compositional erasure. Existing training-free erasure methods treat prompt terms as loosely related routing cues. HGSS instead views concept erasure as the inverse objective to compositional generation. The framework keeps the SS coarse edit interface, but replaces its lexical routing and static conditioning primitives. The two replacements remain training-free: neither introduces learned parameters nor per-concept hand-coded rules. 2. Hierarchical span grounding. To decide what to edit, HGSS introduces a resolver for erase-target spans (Sec. 3.3 ). The resolver combines lexical matches, WordNet-backed taxonomic evidence, and semantic fallback. Broad-hypernym and compound-head guards reduce false positives on preserved objects. 3. Dynamic attribute binding. To decide how the edit evolves, HGSS introduces a per-step conditioning update for early denoising (Sec. 3.4 ). A counterfactual reference defines the target-removed state. An asymmetric attention objective protects preserve spans and suppresses leakage from erase-target spans. 4. Evaluation across complementary axes. The experiments evaluate the two structural mechanisms on compositional side effects, style/object unlearning, and direct lexical safety compatibility. Across the three axes, the resolver and dynamic binding reduce compositional side effects while broadly preserving image quality and the safety capability of the inherited coarse edit. Ablations separate the resolver from dynamic binding (Sec. 4 ). Taken together, the two structural mechanisms view erasure as an inverse objective to compositional generation . Rather than binding every prompt entity correctly, the framework first routes the erase target and its descendants into the edit set, then stabilises the surviving preserve-side bindings during denoising. The grounding cascade and the dynamic-binding update are implemented as a plug-in module for training-free, text-side concept erasure. 2 Related Work Parameter-modifying concept erasure. A large body of work edits the diffusion model itself to remove a target concept. Fine-tuning objectives steer the generator away from the target distribution. ESD [ Gandikota et al.(2023)Gandikota, Materzyńska, Fiotto-Kaufman, and Bau ] fine-tunes U-Net attention with a negative-guidance loss, Concept Ablation [ Kumari et al.(2023)Kumari, Zhang, Wang, Shechtman, Zhang, and Zhu ] matches a surrogate concept, and AdvUnlearn [ Zhang et al.(2024c)Zhang, Chen, Jia, Zhang, Fan, Liu, Hong, Ding, and Liu ] optimises adversarial robustness during erasure. Closed-form and low-rank weight edits act directly on cross-attention projections without full fine-tuning. UCE [ Gandikota et al.(2024)Gandikota, Orgad, Belinkov, Materzyńska, and Bau ] and RECE [ Gong et al.(2024)Gong, Chen, Wei, Chen, and Jiang ] apply closed-form edits, MACE [ Lu et al.(2024)Lu, Wang, Li, Liu, and Kong ] targets many concepts jointly, and SPM [ Lyu et al.(2024)Lyu, Yang, Hong, Chen, Jin, He, Xue, Han, and Ding ] uses one-dimensional adapters. Sparsity- and saliency-guided edits localise the intervention to a subset of parameters. SalUn [ Fan et al.(2024)Fan, Liu, Zhang, Wong, Wei, and Liu ] uses gradient-based weight saliency, SAeUron [ Cywiński and Deja(2025) ] edits sparse-autoencoder features, and ConceptPrune [ Chavhan et al.(2025)Chavhan, Li, and Hospedales ] prunes skilled neurons. Locality-oriented and representation-space methods reduce collateral damage by constraining where the edit applies. CPE [ Lee et al.(2025b)Lee, Lim, Lee, Kang, and Chun ] introduces residual attention gates, GLoCE [ Lee et al.(2025a)Lee, Lim, and Chun ] gates a training-free low-rank adaptation, and AdaVD [ Wang et al.(2025)Wang, Li, Mu, Hao, Liu, Wang, and He ] edits the value space along orthogonal complements. A further line refines target geometry : AGE [ Bui et al.(2025)Bui, Vu, Vuong, Le, Montague, Abraham, Kim, and Phung ] identifies which concepts to push erased samples toward, while CoGFD [ Nie et al.(2025)Nie, Yao, Liu, Wang, and Bian ] explicitly handles combinations of erase targets rather than single nouns. These methods exploit additional parameter capacity to retain preserve-side fidelity, but require per-target training and modified checkpoints. Training-free and inference-time erasure. Training-free erasure preserves the base generator and intervenes only at sampling time. SLD [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] modifies classifier-free guidance using a safety prompt; SAFREE [ Yoon et al.(2025)Yoon, Yu, Patil, Yao, and Bansal ] projects text embeddings away from unsafe directions before they enter the U-Net. TraSCE [ Jain et al.(2024)Jain, Kobayashi, Shibuya, Takida, Memon, Togelius, and Mitsufuji ] steers the denoising trajectory away from harmful regions via a localised loss-based guidance. Semantic Surgery (SS) [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] subtracts a similarity-weighted concept direction from the conditioning hidden states. These methods are deployment-friendly since the same checkpoint serves many erase targets on demand, but their edits are only as reliable as the text-side signals that select the edited span. When the target is reached through a related class, a semantic variant, or an entangled attribute phrase, a single conditioning-time subtraction can fail in two ways. It can miss the routing path entirely, or remove content beyond the intended span. Side effects and robustness. Early erasure evaluations emphasise literal unsafe-content removal and clean-set image quality, exemplified by I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] with NudeNet-based scoring. UnlearnCanvas [ Zhang et al.(2024b)Zhang, Fan, Zhang, Yao, Jia, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Kompella, Liu, and Liu ] expands this view to style and object unlearning across 60 60 styles and 20 20 object classes. SEE [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] factors side effects into neighboring impact , hierarchical evasion , and attribute leakage , each with its own protocol. A complementary line stress-tests erased models with adversarial prompts: Ring-A-Bell [ Tsai et al.(2024)Tsai, Hsu, Xie, Lin, Chen, Li, Chen, Yu, and Huang ] , UnlearnDiffAtk [ Zhang et al.(2024d)Zhang, Jia, Chen, Chen, Zhang, Liu, Ding, and Liu ] , MMA-Diffusion [ Yang et al.(2024)Yang, Gao, Wang, Ho, Xu, and Xu ] , and P4D [ Chin et al.(2024)Chin, Jiang, Huang, Chen, and Chiu ] . Text-side compositional control. A separate line edits text conditioning states during sampling to repair compositional generation failures. Prompt-to-Prompt [ Hertz et al.(2023)Hertz, Mokady, Tenenbaum, Aberman, Pritch, and Cohen-Or ] swaps cross-attention maps between related prompts. Attend-and-Excite [ Chefer et al.(2023)Chefer, Alaluf, Vinker, Wolf, and Cohen-Or ] strengthens the attention of subject tokens that risk being neglected. Structure Diffusion [ Feng et al.(2023)Feng, He, Fu, Jampani, Akula, Narayana, Basu, Wang, and Wang ] incorporates linguistic structure into the guidance computation, and DATE [ Na et al.(2025)Na, Park, Sim, Shin, Bae, Kang, Kwon, Kang, and Moon ] updates the text embedding per denoising step to correct attribute–object misbinding. SynGen [ Rassin et al.(2023)Rassin, Hirsch, Glickman, Ravfogel, Goldberg, and Chechik ] introduces a positive–negative cross-attention loss that aligns each attribute’s attention with the noun it modifies. HGSS sits at the intersection of these lines by keeping the deployment advantage of training-free erasure but replacing the similarity-only routing used by prior inference-time methods with a hierarchical span grounding cascade. From text-side compositional control, HGSS reuses attribute–object binding primitives on the preserve side. HGSS inverts that framework’s objective by first routing target spans and descendants into the edit set, then re-applying binding control only to surviving spans, thereby treating concept erasure as the inverse objective to compositional generation , motivating the counterfactual reference and preserve-restricted attention pair in Sec. 3.4 . 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries and Notation HGSS is described here in the setting of a latent text-to-image diffusion model with a frozen autoencoder, a CLIP text encoder [ Radford et al.(2021)Radford, Kim, Hallacy, Ramesh, Goh, Agarwal, Sastry, Askell, Mishkin, Clark, Krueger, and Sutskever ] ℰ \mathcal{E} , and a U-Net ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} trained for ϵ \epsilon -prediction [ Ho et al.(2020)Ho, Jain, and Abbeel ] . Given a prompt p p , the text encoder returns conditioning hidden states c = ℰ ⁡ ( p ) ∈ ℝ L × d c=\mathcal{E}(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} . At inference, a DDIM [ Song et al.(2021)Song, Meng, and Ermon ] schedule iteratively denoises a latent z T z_{T} over T = 50 T{=}50 steps using classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ Ho and Salimans(2022) ] with scale w w . In our experiments, this instantiation is Stable Diffusion v1.4 [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] . A concept-erasure method takes c c , an erase target T e T_{e} , and an optional preserve target T p T_{p} . It returns an edited conditioning c ~ \tilde{c} such that the sampled image no longer depicts T e T_{e} while the non-target content remains intact. The SS [ Xiong et al.(2025)Xiong, Liu, Ye, Liu, and Xu ] formulation serves as the base: it scores candidate prompt terms against the prompt context through a sigmoid concept-presence kernel parameterised by an inherited offset β \beta and temperature γ \gamma (see App. B.1 for the kernel and threshold values used). The selected weighted spans { ( t k , ω k ) } k ∈ S ⊆ 𝒜 E \{(t_{k},\omega_{k})\}_{k\in S}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{E} (Sec. 3.3 ) then drive a single weighted concept-direction subtraction, c ~ = c − α ⋆ ​ ∑ k ∈ S ω ^ k ​ ( ℰ ⁡ ( t k ) − ℰ ⁡ ( ∅ ) ) , \tilde{c}\;=\;c\;-\;\alpha_{\star}\sum_{k\in S}\hat{\omega}_{k}\,\big(\mathcal{E}(t_{k})-\mathcal{E}(\varnothing)\big), (1) with ω ^ k = ω k / ∑ j ∈ S ω j \hat{\omega}_{k}=\omega_{k}/\sum_{j\in S}\omega_{j} , ∅ \varnothing the empty prompt, and aggregate edit coefficient α ⋆ \alpha_{\star} . In the SS base, selection is similarity-driven and spans contribute uniformly. When preserve spans are grounded, the aggregated erase direction is projected onto the orthogonal complement of the weighted preserve direction before subtraction, at a fixed unit scale. HGSS determines which spans enter S S and their weights and how the edited conditioning evolves during sampling , and does not introduce any new scalar at the coarse-edit interface. 3.2 Overview of HGSS HGSS makes two structural changes to the coarse-edit pipeline, which form two halves of the framework. Structured routing decides what to edit by using hierarchical span grounding instead of token-level similarity (Sec. 3.3 ). Structured edit decides how the edit evolves via dynamic attribute binding during denoising, rather than a single conditioning subtraction (Sec. 3.4 ). The two modules address hierarchical evasion and attribute leakage asymmetrically: structured routing supplies the main erase-side correction, while structured edit stabilises preserve-side bindings so the routing gain is not paid for by leakage onto surviving nouns. The two halves and the SS-inherited coarse edit between them comprise the visual pipeline in Figure 2 . Given ( p , T e , T p ) (p,T_{e},T_{p}) , HGSS executes three inference stages (Figure 2 ; full algorithm in App. A.3): 1. Ground. The span-grounding module returns weighted erase spans 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} and preserve spans 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} in the prompt, using lexical, hierarchical, and semantic evidence. 2. Coarse edit. The coarse edit (Eq. ( 1 )) is applied using the grounded erase spans when available and falls back to the base similarity-driven selection otherwise, producing the static anchor c ~ \tilde{c} . 3. Bind. A text-side localization module builds counterfactual references and preserve-side attribute anchors; during denoising, the dynamic update refines the live conditioning c ¯ \bar{c} with attention and CLIP losses. Figure 2: HGSS pipeline. HGSS surrounds the SS-inherited weighted coarse edit (Eq. ( 1 )) with two training-free modules. Hierarchical Span Grounding produces the weighted edit plan from lexical, taxonomic, and semantic evidence, gated by broad-hypernym and compound-head guards (Sec. 3.3 ). Dynamic Attribute Binding stabilises the preserve-side bindings exposed by the resolver-expanded erase set, refining the live conditioning during the first 0.6 0.6 fraction of DDIM iterations via an asymmetric preserve-aware cross-attention objective (Sec. 3.4 ). The U-Net and the CLIP text encoder remain frozen throughout. 3.3 Hierarchical Span Grounding This module addresses hierarchical evasion : given prompt p p and target T e T_{e} , it returns the prompt spans that should be treated as erase-positive evidence, including spans that are hierarchical descendants of T e T_{e} when T e T_{e} itself does not appear lexically in p p . SS solves this with CLIP similarity alone, which is unreliable when T e T_{e} is not lexicalized. HGSS replaces this similarity-only test with a deterministic cascade that emits weighted (span, relation, confidence) tuples and removes false positives via guard rules so that the remaining tuples become the weighted erase set 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} and, by complement, the preserve set 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} . Cascade. The cascade consults three categories of evidence in order of signal reliability: lexical, taxonomic, and semantic. Lexical evidence provides high precision. Taxonomic evidence expands recall when lexical matches fail. And, semantic fallback handles open-vocabulary concepts beyond the lexicon. These three categories are visualised as the three labelled icons in Box 2 of Figure 2 and are realised through four sources, consulted in priority order. The first source that emits a confident candidate determines the relation label. (1) Lexical evidence tests exact equality, substring containment, and tokenized head-noun match between prompt term t k t_{k} and T e T_{e} . Exact matches are labelled self . (2a) Taxonomic backoff uses WordNet [ Miller(1995) ] to supply non-lexical evidence when lexical matching fails. The resolver looks up synsets for t k t_{k} and T e T_{e} and runs a breadth-first traversal of the hypernym/hyponym directed acyclic graph (DAG) with max depth 12 12 . The closest valid relation is classified as descendant / child (force-include), parent / parent-like , or sibling via shared hypernyms. A broad-hypernym guard suppresses generic ancestors ( entity , object , whole , artifact , organism , …) so that “car” and “apple” do not become hierarchically related through the root of the WordNet DAG. (2b) Activity bridge (a taxonomic refinement) handles verb-style targets and gerund-derived identifiers by expanding each candidate through WordNet derivational links into verb, gerund, and nominal variants, then applying the same relation and CLIP checks. The expansion is generated per prompt rather than taken from a hand-curated activity lexicon. (3) Semantic fallback admits a candidate when its CLIP cosine similarity to T e T_{e} exceeds a stage-specific threshold (distinct values for primary erase, derived modifiers, and activity targets; full settings are in App. B.1). This stage handles out-of-WordNet concepts (style names, brand names) without hand-curated lists. Guards. Two guard rules reduce the most common false-positive patterns in our development set: • Compound-head guard. For a compound noun t k = w 1 ​ w 2 ​ … ​ w n t_{k}=w_{1}\,w_{2}\,\ldots\,w_{n} , the derived head w n w_{n} is only erased if the full compound t k t_{k} has an erase-positive relation to T e T_{e} . A relation between only w n w_{n} and T e T_{e} in isolation will not necessarily trigger erasure. This prevents “ baseball bat ” from triggering erasure under a generic “mammal” target: the derived head “bat” is a mammal in WordNet, but the full compound “baseball bat” does not bear a descendant relation to mammal . • Self-suppression. If the prompt lexicalizes a descendant of T e T_{e} (the resolver returns a descendant / child candidate), the self candidate corresponding to T e T_{e} itself is suppressed to avoid double-counting when T e T_{e} is also a prompt token. The edit plan. The resolver returns a weighted erase set 𝒜 E = { ( t k , ω k ) } k \mathcal{A}_{E}=\{(t_{k},\omega_{k})\}_{k} and an analogously weighted preserve set 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} . The weight ω k \omega_{k} reflects the cascade’s confidence in candidate t k t_{k} : force-included relations ( self , descendant , child ) contribute at a default full weight; threshold-admitted candidates contribute at their cascade-stage confidence score. All other candidates must clear a similarity-confidence threshold and a separate preserve-strength floor that protects against weakly related nouns. When the user provides an explicit preserve target T p T_{p} (as in SEE and UnlearnCanvas protocols), the resolver anchors T p T_{p} ’s span in 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} ; otherwise 𝒜 P \mathcal{A}_{P} is the complement of 𝒜 E \mathcal{A}_{E} within the prompt. All threshold values were fixed once during development and not tuned on SEE or UnlearnCanvas; exact values are listed in App. B.1. The role separation between span grounding and dynamic binding is evaluated through module-level diagnostic ablations in Sec. 4.5 . Worked example. Under target “mammal”, the resolver marks “poodle” (in “a poodle running in the park”) as a force-included descendant span via WordNet backoff. The compound-head guard, however, suppresses “bat” in “a baseball bat on the kitchen counter” because the full compound does not bear an erase-positive relation. The full cascade trace is in App. A.1. 3.4 Dynamic Attribute Binding Dynamic Attribute Binding is not intended to be a standalone erasure mechanism. It refines the live conditioning during early DDIM steps so that, after the resolver-grounded coarse edit, the modifier–noun bindings on spans that should survive the erasure remain intact. A small gradient correction is applied to the conditioning embeddings during early DDIM steps, when object layout and attribute binding are still being established. The update combines two parts: a per-token counterfactual reference and a per-step composite loss. The reference anchors what each token position should encode after T e T_{e} is removed. The composite loss pulls each preserved (modifier, head-noun) pair together while pushing preserve-side keys away from the residue left by the coarse edit. Design rationale. The four loss components in Eq. ( 3 ) (introduced below) are not interchangeable. Each constrains a distinct level of the conditioning pipeline. The update concentrates in early denoising, where object layout and cross-attention bindings are most malleable. Detailed motivation for each component (the symmetric-KL choices for the attention losses, the residual CLIP-space target penalty, and the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} prior anchor) is in App. A.2. 3.4.1 Counterfactual Reference Encoding For each erase span, the prompt is re-encoded with that span replaced by the CLIP PAD token, producing a counterfactual hidden ℰ ⁡ ( p − T e ) \mathcal{E}(p^{-T_{e}}) . The full algorithm is in App. A.3. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Base model and inference. HGSS and the training-free baselines are evaluated as drop-in text-side modifiers of Stable Diffusion v1.4 [ Rombach et al.(2022)Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, and Ommer ] with the DDIM sampler at 50 50 inference steps, classifier-free guidance scale 7.5 7.5 , image resolution 512 × 512 512{\times}512 . No fine-tuning or distillation is performed. For controlled comparison, all SS baselines are evaluated with visual feedback disabled (no-VF). HGSS does not use visual feedback, so the SS → \rightarrow HGSS comparison isolates the two proposed modules under the same coarse text-side edit interface. All reported SS and HGSS rows use the same evaluation protocol and the same benchmark-specific coarse-edit operating point. For compositional erasure (SEE, UnlearnCanvas) the SS coarse-edit operating point is β = − 0.12 \beta{=}{-}0.12 ; for direct safety erasure (I2P) it is β = − 0.06 \beta{=}{-}0.06 , matching the original SS safety operating point. In every setting HGSS introduces no new hyperparameter at this interface and runs at exactly the same β \beta as the matched SS baseline . Per-step refinements use the window [ 0 , 0.6 ​ T ] [0,\,0.6T] and interval Δ ​ t = 10 \Delta t{=}10 . The step size is η = 0.5 \eta{=}0.5 . Under matched inference conditions, the measured per-image wall-clock cost is approximately 1.3 × 1.3\times SS’s on a single L40S GPU at 512 × 512 512{\times}512 resolution. This is consistent with the ≈ 3 \approx 3 extra backward passes derived in Sec. 3.5 . Benchmarks. Three complementary benchmarks were used. (i) SEE [ Saha et al.(2025)Saha, Saha, Gaur, and Gokhale ] served as the primary diagnostic benchmark. Its three side-effect axes isolate the compositional failures targeted by HGSS: neighboring impact (SEE Table 2), evasion (SEE Table 3), and attribute leakage (SEE Table 4). The benchmark spans 11 11 super-categories with 79 79 base objects and 5,056 5{,}056 compositional variants. The official CLIP-based scoring protocol was followed and metrics were reported in the paper direction ( ↓ \downarrow for erase/evasion/leakage; ↑ \uparrow for preserve). Neighbor E E measures residual target evidence on erase-side prompts, while Neighbor P P measures preservation of related non-target concepts. Evasion measures target reappearance through hierarchical or related-class prompts. Attr E E and Attr P P measure pairwise attribute leakage on erase and preserve sides. (ii) UnlearnCanvas [ Zhang et al.(2024b)Zhang, Fan, Zhang, Yao, Jia, Liu, Zhang, Liu, Kompella, Liu, and Liu ] measures style and object unlearning quality. The evaluation covers the 50 50 style targets and 20 20 object targets defined by the official benchmark protocol (selected from the 60 60 -style UnlearnCanvas dataset). The reported metrics are the standard unlearning accuracy (UA), in-domain retention accuracy (IRA), and cross-domain retention accuracy (CRA) triple, with the six-metric average across style and object axes. FID was computed using a regenerated reference set with five images per combination. The SS and HGSS rows are therefore strictly comparable. UA measures target removal. IRA and CRA measure retention on in-domain and cross-domain non-target generations. (iii) I2P [ Schramowski et al.(2023)Schramowski, Brack, Deiseroth, and Kersting ] measures direct safety erasure.
